utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please take the card that's given to you now and read aloud the affirmation that is on it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Smith will first be asking you some questions and then other counsel may have some questions for you. But we'll start with Mr. Smith. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, we're going to be talking about an event that occurred back in 1991 today. And can we go back to, say, January 1991 in Vukovar can you tell the court basically what life was like?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Quite an ordinary life, the situation was all right, everything functioned properly, we all attended school, people went to their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were going to school at that time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how old were you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who were you living with at that time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I lived with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you living?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: In the centre of the city in the family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far is that house from the River Danube?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It is on the banks of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you life was normal early in 1991. When was the first time that you remember that life started to change for you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It started to change after the shooting, that is the incident with the Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about that time what jobs were your mom and dad doing?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother was a housewife, and my father was a private entrepreneur.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that incident in Borovo Selo, did life go back to normal?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: People kept going about their business, although they were a bit afraid of what may happen, but the life went about as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you said they thought about what may happen, did anything happen significant after that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Nothing very significant until the beginning of August when shelling began and the air-raids, and that's when life changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you first noticed that the shelling had begun, can you tell the Court what parts of Vukovar were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The centre of the city. It was the first to be shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know who was doing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know where they were shelling from?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: They were attacking by aircraft and they were shelling from the other side of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From your house, could you see the other side of the Danube?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: From the courtyard, because it is on the banks of the Danube and then one can see the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what -- you said the shelling occurred on the other side of the Danube. What did you see on the other side?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We saw barrels. I don't know whether those were tanks or something else. But we saw that they were firing from those barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stay -- ones the shelling had begun, did you stay at your house on the Danube, or did you move somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Since we were exposed, my father thought it was dangerous for us to stay. That's why we moved to our apartment in a different part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you move to that apartment, approximately?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: By the end of August or early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at that stage was there any damage done to your house or had you moved before any damage occurred?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: A part of the house had already been damaged, and we could not go on living there. That's why we moved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the nature of that damage on the house?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: By shelling. Some shells hit; one hit the courtyard, and another one hit a part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you moved to your apartment block, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We stayed there until we went to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you remember what date, approximately, you went to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My father was wounded around the 16th of November, and we left for the hospital a day after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now about what was life like during the time you were at the apartment for that two or three months that you were in that apartment building. Can you tell the Court what life was like?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Life was such that we were in the apartment all the time. Occasionally when the shelling would stop we would go out to look for food and water and we would return as soon as possible, because we couldn't move freely outside, since there was shelling and shooting. That's why we couldn't move about the city freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how often shelling was for that period of time? Was it weekly, daily?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There was shelling constantly, perhaps there were some breaks in between, but very short ones. The shells fell all the time, and there was firing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did any of those shells hit your apartment block?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Shells were landing around the apartment block all the time. Our apartment block was somewhat sheltered by other buildings, so the houses around it were destroyed or damaged more than the apartment block itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the apartment block and in the area around it, was there any military facilities?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Those were all civilian houses and apartments, shops, and there was nothing of military nature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the time of this shelling, what was your father doing over this two or three months?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My father joined the guards. They were -- there were groups of people on certain streets and parts of the city, self-organised in order to try and protect women and children. He -- his duty was at the Zagrebacka Nama, as it was called at the time, department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is that department store, was that near your house by the Danube?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that your father was injured on the 16th of November. Was he injured any other time apart from that day during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Twice before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell us what those injuries were and, if you know, how he got them?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The first time he was injured he had an entry/exit wound in one of his legs. I was told it was caused by sniper. The other one, the other injury was in his arm, also caused by sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what his last injury, the injury that caused him to go to the hospital on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When he was wounded for the second time in his arm, his entire arm was in a plaster, and that's when he spent his time with my -- me and mother at home. The building caught fire, we were on the third floor, and my mother and myself ran down the stairs to come out of the building. And the fire spread from the first floor upwards. He was on the third floor, and a neighbour of ours could not leave her apartment. He tried to help, and the staircase was in flames by that time. He could no longer go down via the stairs, so he tried to lower himself across the balcony. Since one of his arms was in a plaster, he couldn't use his left arm, and he fell on his legs, injuring his spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he taken to hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was taken to hospital right away. Some of the neighbours tried to improvise a stretcher; rather, they carried him on a door to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the neighbour that he tried to help, did she end up leaving the building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, she managed to use the staircase, whereas he no longer could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the building caught on fire. Do you know how it caught on fire?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Because of the shelling and the incendiary ammunition used. And I believe some things caught fire in the building as there were no windows anymore, and that's why the fire started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you stay that night, the night after the fire in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: In the building next to ours, because that building did not catch fire, and we spent the night in an abandoned apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the building caught fire. Can you tell us whether it was all the apartments within the building or just a few apartments within your building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Most of the apartments burnt down; perhaps one or two was left only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there any soldiers in the building or any weapons being stored in the building as far as you know, in your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Mostly women and children, there were no men at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see your father again that day after he was taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to the hospital to find out what has happened, and I returned from the hospital to the apartment I mentioned, and that's where I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you go to the hospital alone or with your mother or with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I went with someone else. My mother didn't even know that I went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the 16th when you slept that night in the other apartment, did you end up going to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. My father sent someone over to tell us to come to the hospital because there was going to be an evacuation and myself and the mother come to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember what date you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: A day after he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you go to the hospital in the evening or during the day?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was already dark by the time we went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what the situation was like when you arrived at the hospital, in terms of patients and staff and what was happening at the hospital when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The hospital was full of wounded people and beds were placed next to each other. When my mother and I came, we stopped right away, because he was lying on the first bed as you entered the emergency ward. That's where we stayed, and by that time other civilians began coming to the hospital, and soon the hospital was crowded with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many nights did you stay at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: At least two, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why are you not certain that it was two or maybe more?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I'm certain about two nights. I'm uncertain whether there was a third night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the last day before you left the hospital and that last night. On the day before you left the hospital, were you told what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: That morning Dr. Bosanac came to the waiting-room where the wounded were and where we were, and she said that the hospital could not hold so many civilians, that there are a lot of people, and that they should go to Velepromet, because an evacuation was to be organised there as well, in the form of a convoy. But my mother and I remained with my father in the hospital. We didn't want to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what part of the hospital were you in?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As you enter the emergency ward, that's where we were. Before the war it used to be a waiting-room, and it is a waiting-room now. But since they were short of space, that's where they put the wounded, and my father was there, right after getting inside the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were in the waiting-room on this second to last day?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were a lot of wounded. Beds were next to each other, and there were the medical staff and a number of civilians who hadn't left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that day and during the evening did anything of significance happen that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: That afternoon the JNA entered the hospital and the local Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did they do when they entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Those local Chetniks entered first, and they were quite arrogant. They were insulting people. Some of them pointed their guns or rifles at people and then they would move the barrels away, as if they were just joking. It seemed funny to them. They were insulting the wounded. They didn't abuse them physically, but verbally only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was this occurring in the waiting-room?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say local Chetniks entered the hospital, can you explain what you mean by local Chetniks? What were these people wearing?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. They wore jackets, or camouflage pants, but they didn't wear uniforms. They had beards, they had the four Ss and cockades and cartridge belts. They were not soldiers in the proper sense of the word. They didn't wear the same uniform or one couldn't say that they belonged to any particular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say they had beards, did they all have beards?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned the JNA came to the hospital that day. Can you describe what the JNA, what the people you believed to be the JNA, what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. They had olive-drab uniforms, caps with a five-pointed star, as well as the insignia used to be worn by the JNA before the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many of these JNA soldiers did you see, and about how many of the Chetniks did you see?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: First local Chetniks enter the hospital and they were more numerous. I didn't see many soldiers in the hospital except for a few of them when they came to get their own wounded who were treated in the hospital. But most of the people were locals, those who were in the waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did the insulting of the people in the waiting-room go on for?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not long. Perhaps a half an hour, an hour tops. They walked around the hospital. Some of them were looking for some people, greeted some others, but all in all it didn't last for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was there any reason for the insulting to stop? Did you see anything to make you think that the insulting had stopped, caused the insulting to stop?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin came in through the door and introduced himself. He said he wanted them to leave those rooms, and he left two regular JNA soldiers there to stand guard at the door. And he no longer allowed any of those others inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe this person as Major Sljivancanin that you saw? Say the colour of his hair, his build, what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was wearing a JNA uniform. He was tall, slender. He wore a moustache, black moustache, black hair. He had some sort of a cap or something on his head. And he clearly introduced himself, he said, "I am Major Sljivancanin."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long was he in the waiting-room for?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not long. A minute or two perhaps. As long as it took him to say who he was and told those others to leave. He left his own soldiers there. He turned around and left. He didn't even linger at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what time of the day this was or whether it was light or dark?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was dark by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that night did you stay in the waiting-room?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I spent most of my time in the waiting-room. My uncle and cousin were in the cellar a few steps down from where I was. I would go and see them occasionally, but most of the time I spent in the waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what's your uncle's and cousin's name?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Tadija Dosen and Martin Jakubovski Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened the next morning, the day that you left the Vukovar Hospital? The first thing that you remembered occurring.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Next morning, first the nurses came and they gave each of the wounded their personal documents and medical documentation, temperature charts, that sort of thing. They placed the relevant documentation on each of the patients' beds. Then a soldier came in through the waiting-room door with a list, a piece of paper in his hand, and he read from this list names of persons who were to leave the hospital. My father's name was the first on that particular list. However, since my father was unable to walk, we said that he couldn't even get off the bed on his own, that this required a stretcher or something like that. And then my mother asked them to bring a stretcher or something to use to carry him out of the room. Those of the wounded who were able to walk on their own had already begun to leave the hospital. All those who were able to move on their own were to leave the hospital immediately. After a while two nurses brought a stretcher, lowered it beside the bed, and lowered my father's body onto the stretcher. However, they were unable to lift the stretcher themselves because my father weighed a quite a bit. One of the nurses left the room, and after that two soldiers came in, lifted the stretcher and took it out of the hospital. My mother and I followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend's examination, but I think there is something in the transcript. The witness answered a question, and she said all of those who could walk left, including the medical staff, which was not recorded, so perhaps my learned friend could clarify this for us with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They said that all those who were able to walk should leave the room. Everybody started leaving the emergency ward, including some of the staff. They all headed out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened to your father? You said that the nurses couldn't lift him. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Two soldiers came in, they raised the stretcher and carried it outside. My mother and I followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you -- what exit did you leave in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The emergency ward entrance. The entrance and the exit is really the same door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you follow the soldiers and, if you did, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother and I followed close behind them, and once we left the emergency ward they headed left and we just continued following them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In which direction were you going towards?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We headed for that road where the buses were and some rather small lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the name of the road?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It used to be called Bozidara Adzije Street before the war. I think now it's call the Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said there was some buses there and some small lorries. About how many buses did you see?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was a total of four buses there: Two regular buses used for city transport before the war; there was a military bus; and another regular bus there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as you were walking towards the buses, did you see anything on your way?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I saw Major Sljivancanin again, he was standing there with some soldiers issuing instructions to them, telling them what they were supposed to do. We just walked past, so I didn't hear what it was that he was telling them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many soldiers did you see there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Some. I can't be more specific. It was a rather small group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were these soldiers wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: As you walked past these soldiers and Major Sljivancanin, did you see anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Just people leaving the hospital, waiting to be loaded on to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you asked anything as you approached the buses, or your mother asked anything by any one of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. One of the soldiers spoke to my mother to ask if we'd been searched, if anyone had gone through our things. She said that we had been searched and then he told us that we could go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else being searched as you went towards the bus?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As soon as we left the emergency ward to the right, there were those of the wounded who were able to walk lined up against a wall. To the left there was a mound of small items, watches, toothpicks, coins. That's what I noticed in passing. I'm not sure what else was there, but there was a heap of small items there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many wounded were lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were people lined up along the whole length of the wall. I can't give you a figure, but they were quite a large group. The line stretched from the emergency ward exit to the buses, and some of them were, in fact, already getting on to those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where were these soldiers that you mentioned in relation to these people that were lined up?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: From my perspective they were in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened to your father? Where was he taken?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When we left the emergency ward to follow the soldiers, they walked with him as far as the third bus. They tried to lift him on to the bus, but the stretcher was too wide to get it through the door of the bus, so they just lowered the stretcher down beside the bus, and my mother and I remained standing by the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see anyone on this bus that they placed him beside?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were soldiers around the bus and there were two armed soldiers on the bus. Those were the soldiers that I saw. But there were some other persons who were on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Sinisa Glavasevic, Zvonko Vulic, one of my uncles, Tadija Dosen, my other uncle, Ivan Dosen, Josip Kozul. They were on the bus when we arrived outside the bus. It was only on that third bus that people were sitting. The other buses were being filled to capacity and more. But on the third bus there was one person seated on each of the seats inside the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you know any of the people that were placed on the other buses?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I know several people who were there, people I saw there at the time, Sinisa Veber, Karlo Fitus, Ivo Ahmetovic, Ivo Vulic. Those were the people I recognised in that crowd on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that your father couldn't fit into the bus because the stretcher was too big and he was placed beside it. Was anyone else placed on the bus where your father was near?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. As we were standing outside the bus, they brought over a woman who was pregnant, Ruzica Markobasic. Two soldiers brought her from the Vukovar Hospital and started stripping her coat right there outside the bus and rifling through her bag. At one point in time the soldier who was going through her bag placed something into my mother's hand. My mother opened her hand to see what it was, and she asked him what -- "What is this, young man?" And he said, "This is money." And she said, "What would I need her money for?" And then he replied, "You might be needing money, but she is certain never to be needing money again." And then they loaded her on to that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How far away were you from this -- your mother when this happened?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was just next to my mother. This all happened outside that bus, in front of that bus, a yard or two away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Ruzica Markobasic, could you tell the Court whether she was a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. She's my father's cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was anyone else placed on the bus whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Right after she had been put on that bus they brought my cousin, Martin Jakubovski Dosen, from the hospital. They lined him up against a fence, which was near the bus, and told him to spread his legs and his arms, although his arm had been immobilised. He was wearing pyjamas and he was in no position to be hiding anything, but they still searched him. I asked him, "Braco, what's going on?" And he replied, "Don't worry, everything will be fine." And then they put him on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were there was anyone taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When Martin Jakubovski was put on that bus, they took my younger uncle off the bus, lined him up against the fence, searched him, and sent him back on to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you say anything to anyone as this was going on?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Martin Jakubovski what was going on, and he said, "Everything will be fine." That was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did your mother speak to anyone while she was at the bus?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When my younger uncle was sent back to the bus, my mother asked one of the soldiers who were nearby guarding the bus, "Listen, young man, what's going on? What's going on here?" And he replied, "Please, madam, don't ask me." And then she said, "Well, what's all this for?" And he said, "Don't ask me, please. This bus will be swallowed by the night in broad daylight." And then my father started telling my mother in an agitated voice to take me away, asking her, didn't she realise what was going on. And then my mother said, "I can't just continue to walk around like this. I have no one to speak to. I can't just take them away, can I," she said. She was looking around to see if there was anyone that she might approach. I was facing the bus myself, so I didn't see what she was doing or where she was looking. It was after several seconds or minutes perhaps that she walked towards someone in order to accost them, but I didn't see who it was. I just overheard the conversation that she had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which way was she walking? Was she walking back towards the hospital or alongside the buses?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was standing outside the bus, so she might have walked behind my back, because there is no way she could have passed in front of me because of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you overheard a conversation. Can you briefly explain what that was about?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Mom walked up to that man and asked him, "Excuse me, sir, what's my daughter doing here? I can't see any other women or children around here." And the man said, "Who are you?" And she said, "I am Martin Dosen's wife." And he said, "Hmm, I see. Martin Dosen, why isn't he on the bus?" And my mother replied we couldn't get the stretcher on to the bus and that's why it was placed beside the bus. And then he said he would have a lorry there to take the stretcher away. And then my mother asked him if anybody could collect his things. And then the man answered, "He will not be needing those things anymore." He had a quick thought about what he just said and then he asked my mother, "Who do you think is going to be carrying this stuff for him?" And then he asked two soldiers again to come over, and they lifted the stretcher and my mother just lowered his bag on to the stretcher. They went towards the buses and my mother just shoved me aside and told me that we would be joining the women and children who were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you didn't see this conversation but you heard it. Did you recognise the other voice that your mother was speaking to?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: At this point in time I wasn't really focusing on who it was that she was talking to. I was focusing on the substance of the conversation. It was later on that my mother told me who she had talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who did your mother say that she had spoken to?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: She said she had spoken to Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long after this conversation did she tell you that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember when exactly, but I know that it was long after the whole thing was over. I think we were probably back in Croatia by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that two soldiers came to lift the stretcher. Do you know where they took your father?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: They headed for those buses -- or rather, lorries that were near the buses. My mother and I headed off to the right where the women and children were standing, so I didn't actually see them load him on to one of the lorries. I just saw them going towards the lorries, but that was all we saw, and we didn't see anything after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were the women and children standing? About how far away from the buses? Could you see the buses from that spot?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The buses with the women and children, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you were told -- your mother told you to go over where the women and children were standing. Was there a certain place where they were standing, or was it only by the buses, as you just mentioned, these other buses?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As we left those buses, which for the most part had men on them, we passed the emergency ward again and we saw that to the right most of the people standing there were women and children. There were buses there that was on the other side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were those buses parked in the hospital or were they parked on the street?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: They were parked on the other side of the hospital in a street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Ivo Lola Ribar before the war, I think now it's called Zupanijska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that where your father was taken by this third bus there was three other buses as well. Can you tell us who was on these other buses? You said it was mostly men. Who were they and do you know, from the ones that you knew, what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Those I knew were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said mostly men. Were there any women on these buses?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The only woman there was Ruzica Markobasic. The only woman I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened after that? You said you walked towards these other buses on the other side of the hospital. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When we reached the other side of the hospital they asked us whether we wanted to go to Croatia or to Serbia. Mom said we wanted to go to Croatia, and then we went towards those buses that were supposed to drive us back to Croatia. We were waiting to get on to those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did those buses finally leave? Did you finally head towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We boarded the buses and the buses left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stop anywhere on the way, on the way back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We went through the centre of the city, we stopped briefly in front of Velepromet; that was for a very short time. Nobody came off or came on board. Then we went to Negoslavci where we stopped on the road. Nobody left, nobody came. We were simply stopped there for a while. After that we continued on towards Sremska Mitrovica and we spent a few days there. From Sremska Mitrovica we left towards Samac and then crossed over to Croatia. Then to Djakovo and Djurdjenovac, and my mother and I left Djurdjenovac and went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many days did that take?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: In total how many days?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Six or seven days, perhaps, total.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned that women and children were on these buses. Were any men on the bus, these buses that left for Croatia and for Serbia that were on the other side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Mostly women and children. Perhaps a couple or a few men, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said there were soldiers outside the bus where your father was placed, this third bus. Were there any soldiers by the buses where the women and children got on?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I didn't see any. I only saw a few soldiers who stood at the gate of the hospital, but around the bus itself there were not too many soldiers. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say there was a few soldiers who stood at the gate of the hospital, are you talking about a gate closer to the buses that the women and children got on, or a gate closer to the buses that your father was placed beside?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The gate where the buses with women and children were; that's where the few soldiers were. As regards the other gate, there were many more soldiers next to the bus where the men were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This gate where the few soldiers were, were there any other people at that gate?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When my mother and I came from the hospital there were representatives of the International Red Cross there, I believe. They were trying to get inside the hospital. I don't know whether they succeeded or when. We went on towards the buses and they remained behind, discussing, talking to the soldiers there. I didn't overhear their conversation. I just realised that they were trying to get in, but the soldiers wouldn't allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was the gate open or closed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It used to be a gate. It was destroyed by the time. There were just parts left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you some questions about some of the people that you saw on the -- on the buses. You mentioned you saw Ivan Dosen on the bus. Can you tell the Court if he's a relative of yours, about how old he is, and what job he did in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was my brother -- my father's younger brother. At the time he was 30 or 35. He used to live in Vukovar and was single.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what job did he do?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was a construction worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned Tadija Dosen was on this bus, military bus as well. How old was he and what job did he have?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was my father's older brother. There was a few years difference between all three. He was married, had a daughter, he lived in Vukovar, and he worked in the shoe factory, Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he wounded or not?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I should have asked that question about Ivan as well. Was he wounded or not?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Ivan had been wounded as well, but before that. He wasn't in the hospital because of his injuries. He came to the hospital because he heard the rumours in the town that there was going to be an evacuation from the hospital, whereas Tadija was one of the wounded in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned Zvonko Vulic was on this bus as well. How old was he, and is he related to you, and what job did he do?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was around 20 years of age. He used to be a cousin of ours, lived in Vukovar with his parents, and he completed his education a year or two prior to the war. I believe he was unemployed at the time, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned a Martin Jakubovski Dosen as well.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was also around 20, and just before the outbreak of the conflict in our area he had returned from the JNA. He lived in Vukovar, he was single, but he was a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he -- was he serving in the JNA at the time that he was placed on the bus or was he with other -- another military unit?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He did not serve with the JNA, he fled the JNA and since by the time Croatia was in the process of organising its own armed forces, he wanted to remain as a professional soldier and he joined the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Ruzica Markobasic was placed on the bus. Is she a relative, and could you describe whether she had a family?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: She was my father's cousin. She was married, a mother of three, used to live in Vukovar. I believe she was pregnant, five or six months into the pregnancy when she was boarded on one of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you saw Josip Kozul on that bus, the third bus. About how old was he, and do you know what he did in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was my grandmother's neighbour, so I knew him by sight. He was in his early 20s, and I don't know what sort of jobs he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned Sinisa Glavasevic was on the bus. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The only thing I know about him was that he used to work in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, he used to work for Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw some other people you knew on other buses. You said you saw Ivo Vulic. Who is he and how old was he and what job did he have?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Ivo Vulic, he was my aunt's husband. Probably between 35 and 40 years of age at the time, he used to live in Vukovar. I can't remember where he worked, perhaps at Borovo, but I'm not sure. In any case, he was employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you saw Ivo Ahmetovic on the bus. Who was he, what age was he, and what job did he do?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was around 20, my aunt's son. He lived in Vukovar with his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said you saw Sinisa Veber on the other bus. Who was he and about how old was he?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was also a young guy, around 20. I knew him by sight. I knew his name and that he lived in Vukovar, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the last person you saw was a Karlo Fitus. About how old was he, what job did he do?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I used to know him by sight as well. He might have been around 25, living alone in Vukovar, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once your father was taken away by the two soldiers on the stretcher, have you ever seen him since then?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. I never saw any of them, any of those who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, all of those people appear in the annex to the indictment. I would just ask now that a couple of exhibits be shown to the witness. And perhaps if I can ask for Exhibit 156, please. It's ERN number 0462662, and it's a map of Vukovar city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment I'm going to ask you to look on this map and see if you can locate the approximate area where your house was, the place where you saw the gun-barrels shelling Vukovar, and the approximate area of the apartment block in which you moved to. Witness, do you see the exhibit in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And does it look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a map of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your house, the house that was next to the Danube, was that north or south of the Vuka River?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: To the south, towards the hospital, between the Vuka and the hospital. No, that would be to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher just to enlarge the exhibit, which would show -- which would sort of commence, say, just slightly above the hospital and, say, stop just below Nova Ulica, and just have that area enlarged, please. I think that -- that size is quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, now looking at the enlarged version of this exhibit, do you see the approximate location of your house, which was by the river? Take your time looking for it. Can you mark that with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Witness, you said that you could see the gun-barrels on the other side of the Danube, shelling the town. Could you put the approximate location that you could see those gun-barrels?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that with a B, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Where I marked the house. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And Witness, you said that after the shelling had commenced you moved to your apartment block. Can you approximately put the area where your apartment block was?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that with a C, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that apartment block by the river? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that's the Vuka River. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone. The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your apartment block is next to the Vuka River. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I could ask for exhibit number 170.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. If I could ask for exhibit number 170 and page number 5. Thanks. Page 5, please. And the ERN number is 00531260.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the picture on your monitor now?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what's that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see the emergency entrance to the hospital that you referred to a while ago?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you mark that with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you also mark on that photograph with a line the approximate location of the buses that your father was placed beside.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that with a B, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you also draw a line noting the approximate locations of the buses that left the Vukovar Hospital with the women and children, including yourself and your mother?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I would have to make a marking across the roof, because that's on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine, if you can do that, thanks.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Another photograph will show it better, I think, Mr. Smith. Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do that. So that location, the approximate location has been marked with a C. But if we could show photograph 6. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the main entrance of the hospital. That's where the buses with women and children were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And could you put an approximate line where those buses were lined up, please, and mark that with an A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There is a problem with my pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You might be given another colour in a moment.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender that, or both those photographs, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first photograph will be exhibit number 177, and the second photograph will be exhibit number 178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I just have four more photographs to show. If we can show 65 ter number 616, ERN number 00563066, and if only the photograph of the person be shown but not the details underneath, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To object formally, one can see the first and the last name as well as the last time, so the purpose is -- is no longer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we made good efforts earlier to try and avoid this, but unfortunately it didn't work. However, I think this person is I think the cousin of the witness, so I don't think it's too problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, now looking at this picture, do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I do recognise this person. This is Martin Jakubovski Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Witness, you say it's Martin Jakubovski Dosen. It seems to be a double-barreled surname. The Dosen part of the surname -- sorry. Can you explain how Martin is related to you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was my father's sister's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did, in one point of time, did he change his name?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He used to be Martin Jakubovski; that was his father's last name. When he turned 18 he added Dosen, which was his mother's maiden name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did he add that Dosen on the end?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He wanted to. He used to hold my father in very high esteem, and since they shared their first names, he wanted them to have the same last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can call for Exhibit -- sorry, Rule 65 ter number 615, which is 00563067. And if we could attempt to try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand that there will be no broadcast at the moment until it is got into the correct format.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that person on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who is that person?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Josip Kozul.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And he was on the third bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I call for 65 ter number 619, which is ERN number 00563072.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that person on your screen?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who is that person?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Sinisa Veber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He was on the third bus as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. He was on one of the other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can call for the last exhibit, which is exhibit number 158, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who is that a picture of, please?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said that he was on the third bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will -- it is already an exhibit, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right. Your Honour, the examination is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Smith. Now, our tapes have overrun by three or four minutes and must now be rewound. So we must adjourn now to enable that to be done. We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have finished my examination, so unless there is anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the witness. I am attorney Miroslav Vasic, counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Before I begin my cross-examination I would like to ask you the following: Since we speak the same language, please make a pause before you start answering any of my questions so that the interpreters have sufficient time to translate what we are saying. In the summer of 1991 you were 14 years old, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were living with your parents. Were your brother and sister on your mother's side living with you too?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were living at the time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: With their grandmother in Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were your brother and sister on your father's side, from his first marriage, living with you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you in touch with your brothers and sisters, those that I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your brother, Alen Dosen, was he a member of the National Guards Corps in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know if he was or not. I know that he joined the defence of Borovo Naselje. I'm not sure which specific unit he joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was your family in close contact with the brothers and sisters of your father at the time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about your father's brothers? Did they too join Vukovar's defence forces and were they members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they were members of National Guards Corps or not, but I know that they did join the defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you in touch with Ruzica Markobasic and her husband, Davor Markobasic?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. I was not in touch with them on a regular basis. Not before things started happening in Vukovar. I had seen them several months before perhaps, but we were not really in touch on a frequent and regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Davor Markobasic too joined the defence forces of Vukovar and was he a member of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Prior to August 1991 in the house in which you lived with your parents, did you see any weapons lying around?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In June and July in 1991 did you hear any night-time explosions anywhere in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: June and July, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The sixth and the seventh months of the year.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think I heard any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were still going to primary school at this time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I just completed my primary education in late June that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the summer of 1991? Did you leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. I remained in Vukovar throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you at the time for the most part socialise with friends who were the same age as you, your schoolmates?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I did for as long as we could go on functioning and living normal lives in Vukovar; that is, until the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you socialise with anyone at all who wasn't the same age as you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My parents and their friends, their friends who came to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you go to any cafes or restaurants? I mean before armed conflict broke out, or did you socialise in a different way?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was too young to go to any cafes or restaurants. We were just children playing out in the streets, in our flats, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then how come you know Sinisa Glavasevic, who was quite a lot older than you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I met him in the Vukovar Hospital. Because my father knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you meet him at the Vukovar Hospital? Do you remember the day you met?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact day. I know this happened when we arrived at the hospital in order to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he also in that waiting-room on the first floor that you described, where you said you were with your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The waiting-room was not on the first floor; it was in the cellar. I was standing next to my father's bed when Sinisa came. My father and he exchanged greetings and that was how I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you say you met Sinisa Glavasevic at the hospital. But where did you meet Karlo Fitus? He's also older than you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I know him because we ran a restaurant on the banks of the Danube. We would all go swimming there in summer. My brothers and sisters are more or less the same age as he, and we just met by chance. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Vesna Bosanac's sons?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Her younger son and I were schoolmates. We went to the same school, but he was somewhat older. I knew him by sight too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just by sight?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, from school. We would sometimes come across each other in the school's corridors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about her elder son, did you know him too?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I do now, but I did not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that the clashes in Vukovar and the shelling first broke out, first started on the 25th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. I know that it was late August, that was when the shelling started in Vukovar itself. But in Borovo, it had begun a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you were living in your home on the banks of the Danube at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you spend your days in the house or did you take shelter somewhere in order to protect yourselves from the artillery attacks that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We were spending most of our time in the house. But when the shelling became very heavy and dangerous, we would go to our neighbour's cellar, because our house did not have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you decide to leave the house and move to the flat at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was my parents' decision, and they made this decision when the destruction of the town became greater. Our house, too, had been hit by a shell and they decided that it was time to move. We were close to the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this immediately after your house had been hit?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I think so. Very soon after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The building at Olajnica is really a sky-scraper, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Olajnica is a settlement comprising 18 buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many floors did your building have?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The ground floor, five floors, plus the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else from your father's family living in the same building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. My grandmother was living on the fifth floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about your uncle, Ivan? Was he living in the same building too?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was staying with our grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where was your uncle Tadija Dosen living?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: In the centre of town. There are two high-rise buildings there on the very bank of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the National Guards Corps was located in Vukovar, which specific building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I just know the police building, where the police used to be. That was near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what about the Vukovar Defence Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the positions of the town's defenders?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. I was too young to know this sort of thing. I was staying home with my mother, and I know very little, you could say next to nothing, about all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified in chief that there were no military facilities in or around your neighbourhood or any military units. How can you know that if you didn't know where the defence lines were or the defence's most important positions around town?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, but in our neighbourhood I know that there were buildings there, residential buildings, a football stadium, there was a shop there, the hospital was nearby, and there could not have been any military facilities there. I was only telling you about my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is the palace of Count Eltz in the vicinity of your neighbourhood too?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The palace of Count Eltz is next to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How far would that be from your flat at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It's a 10-minute walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While testifying in chief you said that you did not believe that there were any military units or facilities there, just women and children in the buildings. Where were the men? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably somewhere with the defence forces. They weren't with us, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your father joined the town's defence, and you were left alone with your mother in the flat, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your mother ever tell you which part of the front line your relatives, Tadija, Ivan Dosen and Martin Jakubovski Dosen had gone to?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other houses or buildings near your neighbourhood, or were these other houses and buildings across the river?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: What sort of house or building do you mean? Where we lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, where you lived. You lived in a flat which was in a building. Apart from this high-rise settlement, I want to know if there were any other houses in that area or were they all across the river Vuka?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Some buildings were across the river Vuka, but there were some houses on our side of the river too. There were two clearings and then some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How far were those houses from your own neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Between 500 and 700 metres, but I would be hard put to say. It's a five-minute walk across the clearing, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the shelling went on were any shells landing near your neighbourhood or not?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were shells falling all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which period of time are we talking about? When were shells falling on and around your neighbourhood? Can you give us the months?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It started in late August and it did not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So there were shells falling around your neighbourhood in your building throughout up until the 17th of November, 1991. Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It wasn't as heavy at the outset, the shelling, but it became more and more intense as time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you lived in a high-rise, you say there were shells falling near the building. Did you go with your mother to the nuclear shelter at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Mom and I did not want to go to a shelter, there were too many people; it was overcrowded. The sanitary conditions were less than perfect. There was no water, no electricity, and we opted to stay in our flat for as long as we could. There were several neighbours still remaining in our building who had made the same sort of decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about your relatives? Did they stay in the building in their fifth-floor flat throughout?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: At this point in time my grandmother was alone in her flat, and she stayed in the flat until a shell destroyed one of the walls, at which point she could no longer stay, so she went to the shelter at Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But even after this happened you stayed in the flat, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, until it burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to this building and your flat later on. You say that your father was wounded twice by a sniper both times. When was this, and do you know how this happened exactly? How did you know about it? Did your father tell you about any details?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I know that he was wounded twice, the first time around he returned to the flat where my mother and I were, because he was the one bringing us water and food, the bare necessities, and he told us that he had been hit by a sniper. The second time around he came home with a plaster-cast. He told us that he had been shot and released from hospital and allowed to go home. He stayed for several days until the building caught fire. The third time around he was seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you where specifically he had been wounded, the specific locations, the first two times?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you remained in your flat. Were the windows intact? Did you have any sort of heating?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Of course not. No windows, no heating, no electricity, no water. We had planks, our windows boarded up. There was no heating. We were using some sort of a stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You had blankets and planks over the windows, you mean as in windows being boarded up?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that only towards the end, or was it this way from the moment you moved to Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Every day brought new destruction. Sometimes the window-panes were shattered. Sometimes shrapnel would come flying in whenever a shell landed in front of the building. There was always some mending to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: To go back to the day when your building was hit, did your mother ever tell you that the reason why the building caught fire was that the oil that was in the building caught fire after being hit by a shell?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know the exact cause of the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When that happened you left the building together with your mother. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When the building caught fire, we ran down the staircase and came out in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Apart from you, were there any other residents coming down the stairs?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were several. They had already been standing in front of the entrance to the building when we came down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that your father stayed behind to help an elderly lady leave her apartment and that eventually she did come out. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out why he didn't come out together with this lady, since he remained behind?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Because all of a sudden the building started burning from the lower floors up, and he could no longer come down, because the staircase was on fire by the time. She did manage to come down, but it was too late for him. The fire became too strong by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see that, or do you know that from other people's stories?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I saw flames coming out of the apartments below our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask your father whether he tried to leave immediately with the elderly lady?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My father and I never discussed that. We never talked about why he didn't come out or what happened at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you yourself did not enter the building to see the staircase on fire, you can only assume that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. The lady he tried to save and who came out, she said that the staircase was on fire. And then we saw him on the balcony. He was trying to tie a rope to lower himself to the ground. Had he been able to use the staircase, he would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you and the other residents rushed out of the building, did you remain there, or did you look for shelter, since the shelling was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother and I were standing in front of the building. I can't remember what the other residents were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief you said that your father was carried away and that you and your mother remained in that part of the city that day?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We went to the building that was next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
