utterances.text: Can you remember the way your father was dressed when these events took place on that day, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the evening on the 17th did you go with your mother to the hospital for the first time to see your father?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, I went there a day earlier when he got injured. That's when I saw him in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever tell that to any of the investigators of the OTP or to this Tribunal when you testified in another case back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who did you go to the hospital with the first time on the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The first time was not on the 17th but the day when my father was injured, although I am not certain that was the 17th. I can't remember the date, but it was on the same day when he got injured. There was a man or a boy who came with me. I remember that my mother didn't go. She didn't even know I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified here back in 1998 in the Dokmanovic case. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We only provided statements before the Tribunal in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wanted to read out the transcript of that proceedings and what you said then, and perhaps we can confirm the transcript is in English and you will be hearing the translation in B/C/S. For the Chamber and the OTP, those are pages 1066 and 67 of the transcript. "[In English] Did you take then later go to the hospital? When did you go to the hospital? "We went afterwards when the shelling had subsided a bit. My mother and I went to the hospital then. However, they wouldn't let me come to see my father." [Interpretation] Did you state this before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: If it is in the transcript, I must have. But this is in relation to the next day, the day after he was injured, and not the day when he fell off the rope.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that first day when you say that you went to the hospital to see him, did you manage to see him, indeed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I did. I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Very briefly. I wanted to stay longer, but he wouldn't allow me, so I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Had he been examined by that time? Did he tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. As I said, it was a very short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there any shelling that day of the city when you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where was your mother, since she didn't know that you went to the hospital during shelling, since you left the apartment in the neighbouring building and went to the hospital to see your father? Where was she?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother was going through the building to find a place where we could stay the night. And when she was there I secretly left to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How much later after your father's fall did that take place?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Perhaps a few hours later. I left sometime in the afternoon, and I don't know exactly when he fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you return?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Immediately after. I went to the hospital, my father wouldn't allow me to stay, and I returned immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your mother notice your absence? Did she ask you where you were?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, she did, and I told her where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the second time you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother found an abandoned apartment in that building; that's where we spent the night. The next day in the afternoon somebody came to tell us that our father told us to go to the hospital and that there was going to be an evacuation and a convoy organised from there. We couldn't leave right away because there was heavy shelling as well as rain. We packed some things that we had left, and together with a few other people from the building we started moving towards the hospital. It was dark by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That first night when you went to the hospital for the second time, did you spend the night there? When you went there with your mother.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If one could say that we slept any, but yes, we did spend the night in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in Dokmanovic case, did you state that on that first day you returned and that your mother remained in the hospital and that you went back to the hospital next day?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember stating that. My mother and I went together to the hospital, and we stayed in the hospital that day. And the day before that I went there by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wanted to quote another part of the transcript from the Dokmanovic case, page 1067. "[In English] My mother and I went to the hospital then. However, they wouldn't let me come to see my father because they didn't want to tell me that he was immobile. So they took me back home, and my mother stayed on. "Question: I see. Now, did you then later go up to the hospital yourself? "My father told me -- told my mother that evacuation was to take place from the Vukovar Hospital and that we should go back to the Vukovar Hospital together. So on 18th we came to the hospital together." [Interpretation] Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember having stated any such thing. Because there is a confusion in my head in terms of the sequence of events. I don't remember having stated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The few nights you spent in the hospital, where did you spend them and who with?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: The first night when mother and I arrived to the hospital, my mother stayed with the father, next to him, or on his bed. I spent the night with my grandmother on the first floor of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you spent the rest of your nights until the day when the people with the list appeared? That's what you stated during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I spent one night downstairs in the waiting-room. I don't know how many nights I spent on the first floor. One for certain, I don't know whether there were more. But the night before we left the Vukovar Hospital, that's when I was in the waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your uncle, Ivan Dosen, was with you because he had come to the hospital on one of those days, although he wasn't wounded. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he also on the first floor with you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said many civilians came to the hospital, many Vukovar residents, and that Dr. Bosanac told them to go to Velepromet because they should be evacuated from there and that to a large extent most of them left. Can you tell us why your uncle, Ivan, didn't leave with the rest to the Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody could force anyone to go. We stayed as well, my mother and I, as well as some other people. I don't know why he stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out from your mother or your father that after the injury your father was left paralysed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My mother told me subsequently that he was told by the doctors that in case he should be operated any time soon he had a chance of walking again, but they didn't have the conditions necessary for the operation in the hospital, and if that didn't take place, he could remain paralysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And your mother told you that he was told that by the doctors?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, that he was told by the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see him being able to move any part of his body, arms or legs?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He could move his legs and arms, but as far as the upper part of his body, he couldn't sit, sit up. And he also couldn't stand on his own feet, irrespective of the fact that he could move his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us about the soldiers you saw in the hospital. Would you agree with me if I told you that you saw them on the 19th in the afternoon, that is, one day before the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It is possible, I don't know the exact date. I know they came in in the afternoon before the evacuation. I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Today you described two different types of soldiers, the JNA soldiers and the Chetniks. This term "Chetniks," does that correspond to the category you used before in your prior statements when you said they were reservists or, rather, locals from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. But there is a problem with defining a reservist. He could be a member of the JNA, or something else. But those were the terms in general use among the population at the time. There were certain names for Croats and certain names for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand. I just wanted to clarify that the people you termed reservists in your prior statements are now the people you were calling Chetniks. Those were actually people of local origin and paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that -- any such thing as the Serb Territorial Defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I may have, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Dosen. My name is Marina Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Mira Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am one of the counsel for Mr. Radic. I will probably pause between my questions because Mr. Vasic already exhausted a part of my questions, and I will try to revise my list of questions accordingly. You said that when the conflict in Vukovar broke out you lived with your parents on the banks of the Danube. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a 14-year-old girl then. Did you used to play with your friends on the banks of the Danube?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the time your mother was a housewife and that your father was a private entrepreneur. Could you define private entrepreneurship or, rather, what exactly did your father do?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: He was a private fisherman and he had his own catering establishment. He had no employer; he was self-employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did your father own a boat?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you used to take rides on that boat together with your father on the Danube?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a motor boat?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war did you ever cross the Danube on your father's boat?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't go to the other side, but we went to the island in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to reach the island?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991 did you notice some children, some Serb classmates of yours leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Since a number of Serb children were in my class, I noticed that a number of them were absent during the last month of school.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the school authorities ever explain to you why those children stopped attending school?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether the school authorities did any such thing, but I knew that a lot of children used to come from the nearby villages, and I presumed they couldn't come because of the barricades or for some other reason. At that time I couldn't grasp exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you probably asked your parents, what is this log revolution, and what is going on?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As for the term of the log revolution, I am not clear what you have in mind, but I did realise that there was a conflict between Croats and Serbs, because Croatia wanted to become independent.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Croatia's declaration of independence was also mentioned in the statement you gave in 1995. How old were you back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Croatia declared its independence?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it became a UN member?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I know that it was recognised on the 15th of January, 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: By Germany, I believe?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't think it was Germany who recognised us first. I don't know that part of history that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at the time know whether your father was a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, he was. He was an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that when the conflict broke out in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know when your father first became a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the shelling of Vukovar began, you say the shells were coming from the opposite river-bank. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Some from the opposite river-bank and some bombs were being dropped from planes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were shells coming from the opposite river-bank too, right? You said a while ago that it would have taken a couple of minutes to reach the island of Ada. How long do you think it would have taken you to reach the opposite river-bank?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Likewise, a couple of minutes. You can swim across.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how large the Danube is across from your house if you take a straight line across the Danube to the other river-bank?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that probably depends on the water level.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept it if I put it to you that the Danube is over 200 metres across there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It never struck me as that vast, really, because it didn't seem that far. You could see everything on the opposite river-bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in this way that you saw all the barrels that you described on the opposite river-bank, tank barrels or whatever you said it was?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, you could see them firing. We were outside in the garden on our way to fetch water. It was difficult to get any water at the time. And you could see the muzzle flashes from the opposite river-bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When clashes broke out in Vukovar, was it not the case, in fact, that your father was more and more absent from your home?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When the first clashes broke out, they set up some sort of a guard duty in certain streets, certain neighbourhoods, that sort of thing. My father was at the Nama department store. That was his posting, his assignment, because by this time the food supplies had been cut off for the town of Vukovar. There was no food, and whatever food was still available was being distributed to people right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to rephrase my question then. Until the time you moved to Olajnica, did your father spend every night with you in your house on the river-banks?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember about the time we moved, but I know that after we moved he no longer slept with us in the same flat, except when he was wounded. That was the only time he stayed home.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These duty shifts that your father had at the Nama department store, how long were these usually? Day shifts, two-day shifts?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know that much about it. I know that he was there, he was distributing food and he would bring food back home. But I'm not sure how long the shifts were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, tell me, did you ever see your father bring home any weapons to your house on the river-banks; and secondly, did you ever see your father bring home any weapons to the flat at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: My father had a carbine which he had a valid licence for. It was a declared rifle. He kept it somewhere or other in our home. So each time he went to his assignment he probably brought it along. But I'm not sure if he did or not. And he probably kept it out of reach for us, the children in his home. But he did have a clean licence and he owned this rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any short-barrels, something that was smaller than a rifle?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When we moved to the flat at Olajnica, when the shelling turned heavy, and the town's life became difficult, he brought that pistol that he left for me and my mother. He was leaving us alone, he said, and we should keep this for our own protection, but I have no idea where he got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my next question. Did your father ever tell you or your mother when you were present where he had obtained that weapon?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Tadija Dosen and his possible activities or his possible involvement with Croatia's military bodies or units?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: All I know is that he joined the defence when the whole thing began. But must have been in late August or early September. I don't know the exact time he joined, but I know that he did join because everybody was joining the defence forces. Those who had not joined yet were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that all the members of the Dosen family joined Vukovar's defence, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the men?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that all those who had not yet joined any of the defence units were eventually mobilised. Who was in charge of this mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I really don't know, but I know that all able-bodied men were mobilised at some point. I'm not sure who was in charge of this mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that when you moved to Olajnica the building there had no window-panes because all the window-panes had been shattered by shells. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that the windows were boarded up and blankets were placed over it.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember if your father used a piece of plastic sheeting to cover the window and to replace the glass pane, as it were?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what your mother appears to be suggesting in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I have no idea at all what my mother stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you say that after your father's fall from the balcony a makeshift stretcher was made on the spot by using pieces of what used to be a door. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Some planks, splinters of wood, maybe used to be a door, but they used this to make a stretcher to carry him off.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. But this was not a stretcher that was made specifically for the purpose of carrying wounded people. It was just something that they made right there and then as quickly as they could?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps happen to know that all the buildings, especially at Olajnica, had stretchers ready for cases like these?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I'm sure that our building had no stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember what your father was wearing and what you had been doing just before the fire broke out in your building?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what he was wearing. I don't know what we'd been doing. I can't remember at all. Every day was much the same for us, so it's difficult to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what time of day it was when the fire broke out?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in the morning. It was day-time, I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified that the transfer of your father to the hospital building was somehow organised. My question is by whom? Did your neighbours help you with this?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Those were just people who happened to be outside the building at the time because there were many buildings that were ablaze, not just our building. All the residents had rushed out, and those who happened to be in front of the building tried to give us a hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were all of these persons men?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember correctly, I have no time to go back to your transcript now, when answering one of my colleague's Vasic's questions you told us that there were no men there at all.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about our building. That wasn't in reference to any of the neighbouring buildings. Some of the neighbouring buildings were ablaze, and everybody was rushing out of the burning buildings. They just happened to be there and they helped carry my father, take him to the hospital. What I said in my testimony was there were no men in our building.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, fair enough. You say you can't remember exactly the day when your father was injured. You can't, can you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I do know the date, as a matter of fact, because later on I went through some documents that my mother had brought from the Vukovar Hospital. I know that he was admitted to the hospital on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that your father sent someone over to convey a message to you to tell you that you should get ready and go straight to the Vukovar Hospital because an evacuation was in the offing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the messenger was? Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps one of the Dosen family?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I just remember that it was a man, but I can't remember who precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once you were off to the hospital with your mother, you said that there were only women and children in this group of people moving towards the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It wasn't really a large group of people. It was just several people from the building, and we set out together. It was a very small group of women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many people, roughly speaking, would you say?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No more than a dozen, perhaps. Certainly no more than a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know all those people?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Some I did, some I knew by sight, they lived in the neighbouring building.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You knew for a fact that that -- there was a vacant flat in the adjacent building, did you not?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were a lot of such vacant flats. Very few people actually remained in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of the local population at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Having arrived at the hospital, did you go to see your father and stay there immediately?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I went straight to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain to your mother where your father was, since you had seen him the evening before?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As soon as we reached the emergency ward entrance, we saw my father lying there on the first bed in line. She spotted him immediately, and I went up to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once inside the hospital when was the first time you saw Ivan Dosen?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: That same evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I have no idea what we talked about. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When your mother and you arrived at the hospital you spent your first night there with your grandmother on the first floor, or was it in the waiting-room?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was with my grandmother on the first floor that I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which -- was there anyone else in addition to your grandmother and you on that floor?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: There were many people streaming into the hospital that night. It was getting crowded, and that's why the next morning Dr. Bosanac said that people could not linger around the hospital anymore, because the conditions were abysmal, and the room should be made in the hospital, that was what she said, and those who weren't forced to remain in the hospital were asked to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once your father's name had been called out, once your father had been placed on a stretcher by those nurses, once you had left the waiting-room, were both you and your mother searched?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe or say when exactly your father gave you a necklace?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was the day before. I'm not sure about the time of the day, but it was earlier on. I tucked it into my shirt and managed to hold on to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When your father was placed on a stretcher and taken to that third bus, as you described, can you remember what your father was wearing at this time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: All I remember is he was wearing a sleeveless pullover jumper. I'm not sure what else he had on because he had a blanket on top of his body, but I know that it was a sleeveless jumper because he had a plaster-cast down the whole length of his arm, and he could not have worn anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You described the whole sequence of events to us today when your relative Ivan was taken off the bus and then Ruzica Markobasic was frisked. Can you please rerun, as it were, the sequence for us? What happened first and what followed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: All of this happened in a quick succession. Ruzica was brought there and Martin was taken off the bus. It all happened very quickly. It's very difficult to be more specific about the exact sequence. I would be hard put to say, based on my recollection. I did my best describing these events the first time around, but it was all close together. It was a very quick succession of things happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You described a situation where someone placed in your mother's hand some money which belonged to Ruzica Markobasic?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a soldier who was searching her bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what was being placed into your mother's hand?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When my mother opened her palm, I saw something red lying there, but then she uttered it immediately. She said, "I have no use for this money." I saw bank-notes. I clearly saw bank-notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did your mother tell you how much money was there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when representatives of the European Community arrived?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: All I know is that once we boarded the bus with all the other women and children I happened to still have my watch on me. I looked at my watch, and I seem to remember that it was 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. It's obviously a convenient time now to have a break, give the witness an opportunity to have a few moments of peace. And we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honour. Just one short matter. I've spoken to my friend, Mr. Lukic, and he believes that the cross-examination may, in fact, is likely to take the hour, and we're wondering whether or not we could release the witness that is waiting or we can have the witness standing by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, the witness can be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Now, that gives you an unusual liberty, Mr. Lukic. I hope you don't need the full hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all honesty, Your Honour, I hope I'll be able to finish today, so that I don't have to think about things overnight and we continue tomorrow in the morning in any case, and I tried preparing for the next witness during the night before, and believe me, it gave me a lot of headache.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, my name is Lukic. I'm counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin, and I wanted to ask some questions on his behalf. We all know who you are, but there was something missing in the transcript. To be more precise, your name, your name is Tanja Dosen, and your mother's name is Ljubica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clarification for the transcript. In my examination I will mainly refer to the events of the 19th and the 20th of November. As you explained to my colleagues, you -- when you said that you spent the first night in the hospital together with your grandmother on the first floor. And then you spent another night with your father. Why were you not allowed to spend the night with your father, next to his bed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not that I wasn't allowed, but there was simply not enough room. Everything was full of beds and the wounded, and my mother was actually sitting next to his feet on his bed. It was impossible for me to stay. Since my grandmother was in the hospital in any case, I joined her on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that next evening the number of the people in the hospital did not go down, therefore you were forced to stay where you were?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: A number of people left to Velepromet, because Dr. Bosanac said that they should go there and that the hospital could not hold them any longer. So the number of people decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your mother with your father throughout the 19th and the 20th before you left in the morning?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was she present when you saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the door when he came in and introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether -- whether my mother was in the room. She may have gone to the toilet or something, but otherwise she spent most of her time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also present when, on the 20th, in the morning the soldier read out your father's name from the list. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was next to the bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Binazija Kolesar, aka Biba? Does that name tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I heard that name in the hospital, but I cannot put a face next to the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The medical records your mother kept, she also had that with her on the 20th in the morning when the evacuation began?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you were also present there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I spent the whole morning next to my father's bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now go to the moment when your father was put on the stretcher. As I understood that, you waited for him to be put on a stretcher and then all three of you left the hospital. Did you see when other people began going out of the hospital, that is, how much before you started going out?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When the names were called out, my mother said that my father couldn't leave without a stretcher and then the nurses brought the stretcher in. And by that time people started coming out of the hospital, we had to stay there and wait for that stretcher and then he was supposed to be moved from the bed onto the stretcher, and then the nurses couldn't do it and the soldiers came. It probably lasted for some time, but throughout that period people were leaving the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood that as well. But in other words, you cannot tell us approximately what the duration was?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Timewise, as you started moving towards the exit and until you reached the bus, how long did that take?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not long. As one would leave the emergency ward, go through the tunnel, so to speak, although it was actually a corridor, and the time you need to reach the street. We were walking behind the stretcher, and it couldn't have lasted long. We were walking slowly, but we didn't stop anywhere apart from the moment when the soldier asked my mother if we were searched. She said that we were, and then we continued walking to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you reached the bus and your father's stretcher was put down on the ground, and you described the bus earlier, but did you pay attention to what the other buses looked like and whether there were already people on board?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As we were approaching the buses people were getting on already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your today's testimony and in the corrections made to your prior statement, we learned that as you were approaching the buses you saw my client, Mr. Sljivancanin, talk to some soldiers. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the way I read it is that he had already been there before you reached the third bus, and I presume you passed by him?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you confirmed before this Chamber, you testified in the Dokmanovic case, and in the proofing for your testimony you were also shown the statement you provided to the OTP as well as your testimony in the Dokmanovic case, and I wanted to quote briefly some of the things you stated on page 1076. This is the transcript from the Dokmanovic case, the date being the 6th of February, 1998. This was a question put by the Defence and he asked you when you saw Sljivancanin, you answered: "[In English] Well, how much time is needed to get from the basement to the street? "Perhaps about 10 or 15 minutes, and then we stood there for about 15 or 20 minutes when he came, then my mother talked with him." [Interpretation] Do you remember stating this?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And that is correct. Your Honour, may I address you directly? There is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the Dokmanovic case, we gave some simple statements. We didn't go into much detail. Now some things are resurfacing. We are going much more into detail than we did before when I was giving that statement in the first place. My statement concerning the Dokmanovic case was a short one, not very detailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but I think you should just continue trying to help Mr. Lukic with answering his questions. We'll take what you have said into account. Now, I have noticed your -- are you having trouble with your ear-phones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The headphones keep falling off my head. But in any case, I can hear everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think for the most part you could take the ear-phones off and you would hear Mr. Lukic quite clearly. He's got a good, loud, clear voice. So if you wanted to take them off, it will be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe it must be more comfortable without the headphones in any case.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Regarding your question, this is also correct, that he came later, but I also saw him, I passed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Timewise I realise that was quite a long time ago, you were young, and having in mind all the things that were taking place, you must have been quite upset, therefore I would kindly ask you for an answer, if you can give me one. When you reached the third bus, how much time did pass before your mother went to speak with someone? How long were you standing there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We stood there for quite some time. I can't say how long, but some time through all the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did there come a moment when people stopped boarding the buses, when the buses were full? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't remember the buses anymore. I wasn't paying attention, because we were facing our -- that one particular bus. And as regards the events concerning the third bus, that was taking place on the other side, so our attention was there. I wasn't paying attention to the other buses, how many people boarded, who came out, I really don't know. The only thing I know is what I saw in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you can't put any time framework on these events?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude therefore that after -- right after the conversation your mother came back to you and then you went back towards the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. After the conversation we waited for the soldiers who took the stretcher and the father, and my father was taken to one side and my mother and I went to the right, towards the emergency ward, and then we went to the other side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the proofing you were given an opportunity to go in detail through the statement provided to the OTP back in 1995, and you were also given an opportunity to remind yourself of the testimony in the Dokmanovic case, and that resulted in the corrections made to your statement dated two days ago. That's how I came to that conclusion. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the corrections we received, we realised that there was a correction related to what you said today. That is, that you overheard the conversation you reproduced for us today. You said that you heard your mother speak to someone, but that you don't know who that person was, and that then that your mother subsequently told you that she spoke with my client. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I was over-excited and I may have -- I may have said that I heard and that I couldn't see, because my back was turned towards them. I may have used an unfortunate term, nobody reacted at the time. I was quite excited, and -- but in any case, I couldn't see who she was talking to because my back was turned towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on my question, because you've already explained what you're telling us now. Today you told us what you can remember concerning that conversation. We heard your mother's testimony yesterday; you're probably familiar with the fact that she testified yesterday. She never mentioned that Sljivancanin said that your father was to put on the truck [as interpreted], but rather that she understood that he was going to be taken back to the hospital. Is that the way you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I heard him ask why he wasn't on the bus, and my mother said that he couldn't be put on the bus because the stretcher couldn't fit through the door and then he said that they would bring a truck. That's what I heard. I don't know what my mother stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you heard that, but you never saw the person that your mother spoke with?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As that conversation is concerned, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am interested in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Then I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you described, there was some soldiers in front of the bus as well. Did you see any other officer in front of the bus?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. I just saw the soldiers guarding the bus. I didn't see anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your testimony I was given an impression that was very stressful and traumatic for you and that were you crying and that you were upset. Another thing that your mother stated, and perhaps you can confirm that for me, is that after the events she discussed them quite often with you, and she said that you had a lot of questions about what had happened that day. My question hence is the following: Did you discuss the events with your mother in the subsequent years?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. But the way I understood the events could differ from my mother's account. You should ask her what she thought happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am just trying to verify some facts regarding those conversations, and you are here to tell us to the best of your knowledge and under oath what it was that you heard. After the conversation you described for us in detail, your mother came back to you and she was pushing you in front of her to go back to the hospital courtyard. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as you were going back towards the hospital she didn't talk to anyone else during that time?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, she did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you started going back, you overheard the conversation concerning the belongings, and you described that today, that a person said what would he need his belongings for. But did you turn around to see whose words those were?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I did not. I was watching the bus and what was happening there. My gaze was fixed on the people who were on that bus. I was listening to what people were saying behind me, but then I did not turn around to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have a look at the statement given to the OTP in 1995. I will give you both statements in the B/C/S and in English. First we will take a look at the English version. Could you please confirm for me whether on each of the pages of the statement there is a signature of yours?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go to the B/C/S statement. It is not signed, but we will deal with it in some detail. As far as I can see, and I'm asking you if you can remember, on the first page it states that on the 6th of September an interview was made with you. In the original English version, I can see that you signed on the 7th, the next day. Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It may have been so. They came to see us, we were still in exile in a hotel room. It is possible that I signed on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you signed, the statement was read out to you, and you also signed a witness acknowledgement that this statement was given to the best of your knowledge and voluntarily, and there is a signature there as well. Please go to page 3; in particular, the part marked in yellow. Please read it aloud, slowly. We have provided an English copy to the interpreters. So perhaps you could read that portion out for us. Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: May I begin? "At one point my mother went off to speak with Major Sljivancanin to find out what was happening. I could not hear what the conversation that took place because I stayed by my father. My mother returned within a few minutes but did not say anything to me. Two soldiers followed closely. My father was saying, Take my daughter away from all of this. I remember him taking off his watch and giving it to my mother".

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please slow down a bit. You don't need the headphones.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: "I also remember my cousin Martin being brought out of the hospital, and I spoke to him, asking him what was going on. His words to the effect, Don't worry, sister, everything will be all right. Two young soldiers lifted my father's stretcher and started to carry it to another position. My mother was pushing me ahead of her. My father was being carried behind us. I remember her asking someone what would happen with my father's belongings, and the reply was something like, He won't be needing them anymore. I cannot say who said this because it was said behind me."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This statement was shown to you the other day by the OTP, and we now realise that you have made certain amendments in accordance with your testimony today. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In point of fact, several minutes ago you confirmed that you were probably quite agitated at the time and that is what accounts for the discrepancy between your two statements. My question to you now is: Back in 1995 your recollection of everything that had gone on must have been a lot fresher than today. Wouldn't that seem to be a fair suggestion?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: That may as well be the case. It's quite probable, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is something you confirmed to me a while ago. Throughout the years, you talked to your mother a great deal and you discussed the unfortunate events that befell you. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also attended an interview that your mother gave to an investigator of the OTP on the 22nd of August, 1995 in Zagreb. The person she talked to was Dennis Milner. She provided detailed account of her conversation with my client and everything else that had occurred. Did you attend this interview?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was because we were staying in a hotel at the time. It was all happening in one room. I had nowhere else to go. So, yes, I was physically present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were there, you heard the interview, this must have refreshed your memory. And yet 15 days later when you provided your own statement to the OTP, you claimed that you had never heard the substance of a dialogue, a conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin. In fact, you signed that statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: That may well have been the case, but that is not to say that I could not have been wrong. I may have made an error. I may have misspoken or misphrased something. Sometimes it's on account of my agitation that I make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But were you not, in fact, reminded of this dialogue later on when you spoke to your mother?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: We don't really talk about it very often. The images that still haunt me and all the things I remember can never be changed. Even if I discussed this with my mother, what I experienced, what I saw and heard back then, I'm not saying that I can't be wrong about details, but all these images that will stay with me cannot be changed in any way. My experience was one thing; my mother's experience was a different thing altogether. We are two different persons. Our stories are alike because we were both there physically, same place, same time, and we experienced the same things. Can't be that different, because we were both there. The place was the same, and the persons, the protagonists were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just several questions in relation to this statement. You can have some time to go through it, if you like, but if you can just tell me whether at any point in that 1995 statement you mentioned the fact that Sljivancanin had arrived at the hospital on the 19th and introduced himself to you. Did you mention this at any point in time in your statement?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I may not have mentioned that, just because it was a perfunctory statement that was taken. In the Dokmanovic case my mother testified before me, and she probably gave a more substantial account. When I appeared, I was asked a number of perfunctory questions, and the issue of the time-line was not raised as it has been here today. This is a perfunctory statement. It is not a very thorough statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, as far as what you said about the Dokmanovic case. It was a different person that was involved there, that is true. But this statement was taken back in 1995, and the person investigated was my client. Did Milner ask you anything about Mr. Sljivancanin, my client, or did he only ask you questions about Mr. Dokmanovic, who was on trial back then?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: When I appeared here to testify, no one asked me anything about your client. This statement was produced based on the account I then gave of what had occurred. That is how this statement came about. I wasn't interviewed or examined in great detail about anything. It was about the Dokmanovic case back then and it was not only to do with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can leave the statement for the time being, I have several questions left. Does the name of Darko Vuk, aka Drka [as interpreted], ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does. But seeing as my father owned a boat, I think this was another person who also owned a boat that bore the same name. I may have seen this person at one time or another back then. I may have known the person by sight, but nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked today about walking together with your mother and father. As you were passing through that tunnel, so to speak, on the way out of the hospital where people were being searched and eventually reaching Gunduliceva Street, said you saw both buses and lorries when you got there. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, buses and lorries of sorts, small ones. Military ones. Or, rather, they were olive -- well, you know, dark ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us please go back for a minute to that photograph, if I could just have a clean copy, please. This is Exhibit 173, if I'm not mistaken. And -- just a minute, please. The photograph is from a set. This is 170, and the photograph number is 5. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 00531260. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please take that electronic pen again, if I can have the usher's assistance, please, to help the witness. It's right behind the screen. We will just tackle this briefly and then we're about to conclude. You drew a sketch for the Prosecutor, you marked the position of the buses. What I want to know is: Can you specify by using this photograph the exact spot where you were with your father, where was the third bus?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was around here. The first, the second, and then the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you put a letter A there, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks]. There was no gate here and you could just drive straight through. We were standing here, on this side, just outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that your mother had gone off to speak to my client. You probably didn't see her return or where she returned from. If you did, can you please put an arrow there?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It wasn't like she that went anywhere far. It was a stone's throw from where we were standing. We were standing outside the bus, because that's where they laid down the stretcher. It was a stone's throw from where we were standing, perhaps one or two metres. It's not that she walked away in order to go somewhere and speak to someone, she was right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you see Mr. Sljivancanin as you were leaving the hospital compound and going towards the buses? Where was he standing? Can you put a letter B there, please.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was around here, because we passed this spot on our way to the buses. And this is the location, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any wounded lying in this area outside the bus on that day, any other wounded?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I wasn't really paying attention, but I don't think so. I saw those who were lined up against this wall, but none of them were lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have this photograph admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under the reference 182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another clarification about something that you raised today in your testimony. When you headed back to the hospital, the main entrance, if you like, where all the other women and children were, my understanding is the buses were there, and you immediately went to those civilian buses, as it were, that later drove you away?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we walked back through this passage, walked all the way back to the emergency ward. They asked us if we wanted to go to Croatia or to Serbia, mom said Croatia, and the buses were there already waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have one general question stemming from some of your answers while being cross-examined by my learned friends. You say that you knew some of the persons mentioned by the OTP, Zvonko Juric, Josip Kozul, Sinisa Veber, Ivo Vulic, Karlo Fitus, Ivo Ahmetovic. Did you know at the time these persons had been in any way involved with Vukovar's defence?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: As I said before, those who didn't join of their own free will were mobilised. Therefore, I am certain that all these persons in one way or another took part in the town's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was just something I based on one of your previous answers, but thank you for clarifying the issue. Just a minute, please. You also say that you met Sinisa Glavasevic at the hospital when you came there to see your father. Had you ever seen him before then?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Virtually the first time you saw him was then, and after that you saw him on the bus, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, on that third bus. All I knew was he had been working for Radio Vukovar. I was familiar with his voice from a time while we were still able to listen to the radio, but then I met him properly at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember exactly what he was wearing first in the hospital and then on the bus later on?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No detail that sticks in your mind?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. So many people passed through that hospital that I'd really be hard put to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You identified Sinisa Glavasevic in that photograph based on your memory of him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to which I have seen a number of his photographs over the years. There is some sort of a book that was published, Sinisa Glavasevic's memories, or memoir, so I saw a photo of him that was published in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose in those photographs he looked much the same as in the photograph that you were shown today, right?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I suppose the photographs date back to the same years because they couldn't have taken any photographs of him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was the same age as he was when you saw him at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Smith, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a few quick questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in answer to my learned friend's question that in the 1995 statement you said you may not have mentioned Mr. Sljivancanin in the hospital the night before you left. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now going to read you a small passage from the Dokmanovic case dated the 6th of February, 1998 at page 1076, and it's the evidence that you gave in that case, and I would like you to say whether you agree that you said that. "And my last question" - this is at line 11 - "at what time did you last see Major Sljivancanin? "I do not know exactly what time it was, but I just know that it was on the 19th of November, before the evening began. "I'm asking about the 20th. When did you first see him? You went out at 7.00? "Yes, we went out at 7.00. "And when did you see him? Well, how much time is needed to get from the basement to the street? "Perhaps 10 to 15 minutes, and then we stood there for about 15 or 20 minutes when he came. Then my mother talked to him." Do you agree that that was your evidence in the Dokmanovic case? If you are unsure, just say, I am unsure, but yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And one last question: When the statement was taken in 1995, can you tell the Chamber about how long it took for the investigator to take that statement in terms of hours, if you can.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: It only took a very short while. It was a superficial summary of what had occurred. They only took a short time taking that statement, and that's why the statement is the way it is. I think they focused much more on my mother's statement than on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, it's a two-page statement. Do you have any indication of how many hours it took to take? And if you don't know, just say, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm checking the English and the B/C/S at the same time to see if there are any major differences, that's why I decided to object. The text of the English is two pages long; the B/C/S is two and a half pages. Just because the OTP take of the English version proves to be very accurate, but mine wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that the English statement is two pages, the one that you signed?

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could answer my question, can you indicate about how many hours it took to take the statement? And if you can't say, just say, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: TANJA DOSEN
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember. I know that it was very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. You will be pleased to know that that is the end of your evidence. I know it's been a long day for you, but you are now at the end of the questioning. We would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to help us and for the evidence that you have given. When we rise now, you will be guided out, but you will be free then to go back home when you wish. So thank you very much for your help. We resume at 9.00 in the morning, and the last information I have is that we continue in this courtroom. We don't move to any other courtroom. So 9.00 tomorrow morning here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.51 p.m.,
